rows.answer:
You can technically push a Friday deploy, but it isn't off limits. It needs approval from the on-call engineering manager first [1][2]. The regular deploy window is Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific, so a Friday deploy is outside it [2].

Other points that apply:

- **Rollbacks** are allowed at any time without approval [1][2].
- **Canary bake** is now 45 minutes, up from 20, before a deploy can be promoted automatically. Promotion also requires two new checks: no sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers, and runner consumer lag growing by no more than 2 minutes [2].
- **Data-plane changes** (`ingest/` or `runner/`) roll out in waves, with 30 minutes between waves, so a data-plane deploy takes about two and a half hours to reach every cell [2].
- **During an incident**, the incident commander can approve skipping the bake with `/deploy expedite`, and that is logged in `#eng-changes` [2].

Critical lab results must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes. If that clinician can't be reached within 30 minutes, the result goes to the on-call medical director [1].

**If you can't reach the ordering clinician:**

1. Keep trying the ordering clinician until the 30-minute mark [1].
2. Escalate to the on-call medical director. Call the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2 [2].
3. The answering service pages the on-call medical director. If there's no callback within 10 minutes, it pages the backup [2].
4. Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers. Pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which the chart documentation needs [2].

Whoever notifies someone must document the critical result in the chart with the time and the person notified [1].

**Related timing:** A critical lab value called in by the reference lab is a separate trigger. It requires notifying the supervising physician within 30 minutes [1].

No. Removing the name doesn't make it allowed. The approved-AI-tools policy says public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants are not approved on any device, and that "de-identified" is not a loophole: removing a name is not enough to make a case non-identifiable, so treat any patient details as PHI [1].

None of the approved tools is a general summarizer for patient histories:
- **Quillon Ambient** is approved for PHI, but only drafts visit notes from the conversation, at the Riverside and Elm Park pilot clinics [1][4].
- **Meridian draft replies** is approved for PHI, but only drafts portal message replies inside Meridian EHR, and a clinician must edit or approve each one [1].
- **Halcyon Assist** answers policy questions only, and you must not paste patient details into it, even without names [1].

If you need a patient's history, use Meridian EHR, which is the approved system for the full clinical record [5].

If you have already pasted patient information into a public chatbot, report it to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [3].

rows.answer:
**17 lab results** were filed into the wrong patient's chart in the Bayline incident (RCA-26-07). The events ran from July 21 to 23, 2026, at the Riverside and Northgate clinics, and all 17 were moved to the correct charts by July 24 [1].

The root cause analysis identified three contributing causes [1]:

- **Weak fallback matching:** When the MRN was missing, Switchyard matched results on last name and year of birth only. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume.
- **No monitoring:** Nobody was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were using the fallback rule.
- **No change-notice obligation:** The Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes.

The trigger was a change Bayline deployed to its results feed on July 20. It moved the MRN into a different HL7 segment without notice. The interface engine then could no longer find the MRN and fell back to the weak matching rule [1]. A medical assistant at Riverside caught a potassium result that didn't match the patient's history, and the feed was stopped on July 23 [1]. Two patients had abnormal results go to another chart, and their follow-up was delayed by four and six days. Neither suffered lasting harm [1].

A fix is in progress. Project Heron, a positive patient identification check before lab results are released to the patient portal, is listed as RCA-26-07 action 4. It is build-complete and awaiting release, with a Q4 2026 target [6].

The closest equivalent is a **root cause analysis (RCA)**, which must be **completed within 45 calendar days** of the event becoming known [4]. Unlike the Northwind postmortem, which is counted in business days, this deadline is in calendar days.

Related Halcyon deadlines for a serious event:

- **Charter:** QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours [4].
- **Notify the on-call medical director:** for a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies them within 1 hour [4].
- **Report:** anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a report in SafeReport [4].

The RCA applies to every Level 1 and Level 2 event [4]. The excerpts I have don't define those levels, so check the policy's level definitions to confirm whether a given event qualifies.

Halcyon needs two things in place before a vendor receives patient data: a signed business associate agreement (BAA) and a completed security risk assessment. Both are required before any PHI is disclosed, including test files or a small pilot.

- **BAA:** A vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI for Halcyon is a business associate, and a signed BAA must exist before any disclosure [6].
- **Security risk assessment:** New systems that will hold PHI need one, plus a BAA if a vendor is involved, and an entry in the clinical and business systems inventory before go-live [8][7].
- **Other steps for AI tools:** Any tool that will handle PHI also needs a clinical safety review by the CMIO if it is used clinically [7].
- **Timing:** The Privacy Officer and HIPAA Security Officer should be engaged early. The typical turnaround for an AI tool is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [7].

The clearest example is Tallgrass Survey Co. (proposed). Its BAA is not executed, so no PHI may be shared, even though its security risk assessment passed with conditions in September 2026 [6].

Some vendors in the business associate register show blank BAA or risk assessment fields, including Brightwater Billing Services and Polyglen Interpreting. I could not confirm whether those are missing or simply not recorded, so check those files directly before sharing data [4][1].

rows.answer:
Northwind has a close equivalent, but it covers a different situation. Its "emergency access" lets support or on-call engineers reach a customer's workspace, not a patient chart. The two work quite differently.

**Halcyon (break-the-glass to the Meridian EHR)**
- Used when a chart is outside a clinician's normal treatment, payment or operations relationship, for example an unscheduled walk-in or covering for a colleague [1].
- The user picks a reason and types a justification. No one approves it in the moment [1].
- Access lasts until the end of the shift, up to 12 hours [1].
- The Privacy Officer's team reviews every event within 2 business days, and the manager is asked to confirm unclear reasons [1].
- Misuse is a privacy incident and can lead to termination [1]. Monthly compliance reviews also use anomaly detection on EHR logs [4].

**Northwind (emergency access to customer workspaces)**
- Used only with an open support case or declared incident. "Curiosity" or "it would be faster" are not valid reasons [2].
- Requires approval before access is granted: a second engineer from support or on-call must approve in Teleport, and cannot be on the same case [2].
- Access is read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent first [2].
- Expires after 2 hours, deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour production session [2].
- Every session is recorded and kept for one year. The customer's audit log shows the access, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours. Security reviews a sample of sessions weekly, plus every session that used write access [2].

**Key differences**
- **Approval:** Halcyon has no pre-approval, because patient care comes first. Northwind requires a second engineer to approve beforehand.
- **Duration:** Halcyon allows up to 12 hours; Northwind allows 2 hours.
- **Review:** Halcyon reviews within 2 business days; Northwind's sessions are recorded and sampled weekly, and the customer is notified.
- **Trigger:** Halcyon's is clinical need for a patient; Northwind's is a support case or incident.

Northwind's general production access is separate. It runs through Teleport with 8-hour sessions and no standing database access [3].

**Short answer: No for restricted data or patient data. At Northwind, confidential data can go in Slack on a need-to-know basis. At Halcyon, Slack is never allowed for PHI.**

**Northwind Labs**
- Restricted data never goes in Slack. That covers customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys, which never leave production [1].
- Confidential data (financials, contracts, employee data) is shared on a need-to-know basis [1]. The policy doesn't name Slack for this class, so check with your team if you're unsure.
- If you see unexpected data, such as another customer's data during emergency workspace access, stop and report it in `#security-help`. Don't paste it into Slack [4].

**Halcyon Health**
- PHI may only be stored in the EHR, the practice management system and approved systems on the intranet. Slack is explicitly excluded [2].
- The systems inventory says Slack is "Never, including DMs" for PHI [3].
- Other channels that are also off-limits for PHI include email subject lines, personal notes apps, and AI tools not on the approved list [2][3]. Use the EHR's secure messaging for patient communication [2].
- Report a suspected privacy incident to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours, at privacy@halcyon.example or via the compliance hotline [2].

You need two sign-offs, plus an ADR if the change alters how long data is kept.

1. **Platform change approver: Oluwaseun Adeyemi.** Driftwood, the archive where these events live, is owned by PLAT [6]. Lifecycle rules and retention settings are normal changes, which need sign-off from the change approver of the owning team [3]. PLAT's delegate is Kofi Mensah [7].
2. **Head of Security: Tomasz Wierzbicki, or the security on-call delegate.** Driftwood is classed as Restricted data [6]. Normal changes to a Restricted service also need Head of Security or the security on-call delegate [3].

Other requirements:
- **ADR:** any change that alters how long customer data is kept needs an ADR, linked from the PR [3].
- **Customer notice:** shortening retention needs 30 days' notice from the account team for Enterprise contracts that reference a retention period [3].
- **Process:** add the `change:normal` label, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request review from the approver as a CODEOWNERS reviewer. Approvals expire after 7 days [3].

For context, the current archive default is 365 days in the v2 retention standard, which took effect September 15, 2026 [2]. The Security team owns that standard [2].

**Who signed off:** The helpdesk is Hollowpine Software's ticketing and help-center tool. Its DPA is not signed. Interim cover is security exception SEC-EX-117, approved by the Head of Security on August 24, 2026 [1]. The Head of Security is Tomasz Wierzbicki [8].

**How long it lasts:** The information security policy says exceptions require written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [6]. Counting 90 days from August 24 gives about November 22, 2026. That is my calculation, not a date the register states. Today is October 31, so about three weeks remain.

**What happens at expiry:** If the DPA is still unsigned, Support Operations must either get the exception renewed or move ticket intake back to email [1].

**Status of the DPA:** The draft arrived in July 2026, and redlines with legal have been open since August. The main open point is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model [1]. The security review is a conditional pass, which requires AI reply suggestions to stay disabled until the DPA is signed [1]. The contract renews January 31, 2027 [1].

Changing the reminder send time is a significant change, so it needs three approvals:

1. **System steward: Felix Brandt.** Pillbox, the medication reminder scheduler, is owned by Digital Health Engineering — Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), and Felix Brandt is that team's steward [7][1].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off: the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei** [1].
3. **Review at the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB)**, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1]. Changes go to CSCAB as a change request with a CHG number [2].

Patient-facing automation such as reminders is classed as significant under the policy [1]. Any change to reminder timing also has to respect the idempotency key that stops a reminder from being sent twice, which was adopted after the duplicate-reminder incident IR-0412 [5].

rows.answer:
The fix would go through **Integration Services (INT)**, the team that owns the Bayline feed into Switchyard, the interface engine that misfiled the results. Because the fix changes results routing, it is a significant change and needs three approvals:

1. **System steward:** Owen Mbeki, for Integration Services [2].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off:** CMIO Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [2].
3. **Review:** the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB), which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2].

The root cause analysis points at Switchyard's fallback matching on last name and year of birth [1]. Switchyard is built in-house with no outside vendor, and the Bayline HL7 feed into it is owned by INT [5]. The fix to the feed mapping and the fallback rule therefore sits with INT.

Two notes:
- The on-call medical director can approve an emergency change to stop ongoing patient harm, with CSCAB reviewing at its next meeting [2]. That route only applies to an urgent stop-gap, not to a permanent fix.
- The RCA says the MRN mapping was corrected on July 24 [1]. The approvals above apply to the permanent fixes the RCA calls for, such as monitoring fallback-matched messages and a change-notice obligation with Bayline. The knowledge base doesn't say whether those fixes have been approved yet.

Three of the four INC-2291 follow-up actions are confirmed as done. The fourth, item 3, has a confirmed shipping date, but the postmortem's status markers are less certain than they look.

- **Item 1, validate certificate chains in the rotation job (platform team, due Aug 28):** marked done in the postmortem [2].
- **Item 2, lower the canary handshake-failure alert (ingest team):** marked done [2].
- **Item 3, cut gateway TLS session ticket lifetime from 4 hours to 30 minutes (ingest team, due Sep 15):** the September 12 changelog says it shipped ahead of the due date [4].
- **Item 4, add a "TLS handshake errors" dashboard panel (observability):** marked done [2].

The postmortem's "done" markers are the main evidence for items 1, 2 and 4, and it's unclear when they were added. The document is stamped August 14, but it records completion of items due August 28 and later, so it was evidently edited after that date. Nothing I found gives a completion date for those three items.

The Q3 board update says "all action items are on track" [3]. That describes status as of the board update, not completion, so it doesn't confirm that anything shipped.

The October deploy pipeline changes also respond to the incident: canary bake time rose from 20 to 45 minutes, TLS handshake checks were added to promotion, and data-plane deploys now roll out in waves [6]. That note doesn't say whether it counts as a formal action item from the postmortem.

- **Deletion requests** must now be completed within 14 days, down from 30 [2].

The sales pricing policy still says custom retention beyond 400 days needs security approval [3]. That predates the v2 change to 365 days, so it may not reflect the current limits.

You have **14 days** from the verified request to complete deletion in all live systems. This comes from version 2.0 of the customer data retention standard, effective September 15, 2026, which cut the window from 30 days [2].

Key points:
- **Live systems:** deletion must be completed in all live systems within 14 days [2].
- **Backups:** these are not deleted early. They age out on the normal 35-day backup schedule [2].
- **Logging:** Support logs every request in the `data-requests` queue, which alerts at day 10 [2].

The older v1 standard (February 2026) said 30 days, but v2 supersedes it [1][2].

rows.answer:
When a customer goes over their limit, the API rejects the request with **HTTP 429** [1]. The response includes a **`Retry-After` header** giving the number of seconds to wait before retrying [1].

**How the limits work**
- Limits are per workspace, not per API key. Ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- Short bursts up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].
- Limits vary by endpoint and plan. For example, event ingest (`POST /v2/events`) is 100 req/s on Starter, 2,000 req/s on Growth, and 10,000 req/s on Enterprise by default [1].

**How customers know when to retry**
- Northwind's SDKs read `Retry-After` and back off automatically with exponential backoff [1]. Customers using the SDKs don't need to write their own retry logic for 429s.
- Customers calling the HTTP API directly should read `Retry-After` themselves and wait that long before resending. The source says the SDKs honour the header; it doesn't spell out direct-API guidance beyond the header itself, so confirm with the docs if needed.

**Related cases to keep separate**
- Endpoints not included in a customer's plan return **HTTP 403**, not 429 [1].
- A 503 is a service-side failure, not a rate limit. During the August 14 ingest outage, events were rejected with 503 and customer SDKs retried them [3].

- **runner**: executes customer pipelines. Stores partition state in local RocksDB and reference-table snapshots. Owner: DP [1].

rows.answer:
No, don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand for us-west. The runbook step is out of date. Hydrant, the autoscaler, has managed gateway replicas in us-west since October 15, and it replaces that manual step [1][3].

- **A manual scale will be reverted.** Hydrant treats the replica count as its own and reverts manual changes within 2 minutes [3].
- **Hydrant should already be scaling.** It scales up when average gateway CPU stays above 65% for 3 minutes, adding 25% of current replicas (at least 2) per step [3]. Your 80% reading is above that threshold.
- **If you need to pin the count**, for example while debugging a bad gateway build, use `nwctl hydrant hold --cell us-west --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. Holds last at most 4 hours and need no approval. Release early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell us-west` [3].
- **Watch the ceiling.** us-west's Hydrant range is 10 to 48 replicas [2]. If the cell sits at the ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call, because that usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [3].

The rest of the runbook's "Ingest 5xx rate above 1%" steps still apply. Check which cell is affected, and look at gateway TLS handshake errors (see INC-2291) [1][3].

For a Growth workspace, the legacy `/v1/track` endpoint allows **500 requests per second** [1]. The limit applies per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in one workspace share that budget [1].

Some related details:
- **Bursts:** Short bursts of up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- **Over the limit:** The API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [1].
- **No raises:** Legacy `/v1/track` limits won't be raised for anyone. Customers should move to `/v2/events`, which SDKs released after March 2025 already use [1].
- **Shutdown:** The endpoint stops accepting events on April 30, 2027 [2].
- **One-off backfill:** The DP on-call primary can grant a temporary raise of up to 72 hours on any plan that has the endpoint [1].

An Enterprise workspace can force a reference-table snapshot rebuild once every 2 minutes, via `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh` [1]. Limits are per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in the workspace share that one allowance [1].

The source says a forced refresh discards the runner's snapshot and rebuilds it with a full table scan, which is expensive for large tables. It also says most customers never need one, because snapshots are kept current with change data capture [1]. The contract-based increase for Enterprise covers only the event ingest endpoints, so the source does not show a way to raise the refresh limit [1].

rows.answer:
If your annual training is still open, the 14-day grace period is what matters. The policy says the annual HIPAA training is due by January 31, and clinical system access is suspended automatically once training is overdue by more than 14 days [1]. So you have until 14 days after the deadline before the lockout.

Today is October 31, 2026, so the timing depends on which deadline you're measuring against:

- **If you're working toward the January 31, 2027 deadline,** you have until about February 14, 2027 before suspension applies [1].
- **If you're behind on a deadline that has already passed** (January 31, 2026), you're well past the 14-day window. Your access may already be suspended or be suspended automatically, so check with your manager or the compliance team now [1].

Completing the training clears the overdue status. Access is then restored, but I don't have a source on how long restoration takes, so ask compliance for that.

rows.answer:
**No, don't throw the vaccines out.** At 10 °C the fridge is outside the required 2–8 °C range, so the stock must be quarantined, not discarded. Do not use it until the clinical pharmacist decides [1].

1. **Don't discard anything.** Label the affected stock "Do not use." Keep it refrigerated in a working unit, and record the reading, the time and how long the fridge has been out of range [1].
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** The pharmacist checks with the manufacturers whether the stock can still be used [1].
3. **File a SafeReport.** It is a Level 4 near miss if no vaccine was given. It is a higher level if a patient received vaccine from the affected stock [1].
4. **Give no vaccine from this stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [1].

Frozen vaccines are never refrozen or reused once thawed [1].

If you can't reach the clinical pharmacist and need a clinical decision, the on-call medical director can advise on any clinical question a supervising physician can't resolve. Call the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2 [4].

Three languages missed their connect-time target on average in Q3 2026 (July–September): Vietnamese and Arabic in the 2-minute tier, and Somali and Karen in the 5-minute tier. Vietnamese and Arabic exceeded the 2-minute target, and Somali and Karen exceeded the 5-minute target. Wait, that's four languages, so here is the corrected list:

- **Arabic (2-minute tier):** average 2:12 against a 2-minute target [1]
- **Somali (5-minute tier):** average 5:40 against a 5-minute target [1]
- **Karen (5-minute tier):** average 6:18 against a 5-minute target [1]

Every other listed language met its target on average. Haitian Creole, in the 5-minute tier, averaged 3:54 [1]. The "all other languages (61)" group averaged 3:31 [1].

The report compares average connect times with the targets. It does not give the share of individual sessions that connected within target, so a language could have met its average while still having slow sessions. Clinical Operations plans to raise every language that missed its target at the Polyglen renewal discussion in November 2026 [1].

rows.answer:
Halcyon charges nothing for a no-show. The October 2026 revision eliminated the no-show fee, effective October 5, 2026 [1]. Any no-show fees billed before that date that are still unpaid are waived, and front desk staff should not try to collect them [1].

The $25 fee in the 2025 policy no longer applies. That policy charged it after the second no-show in 12 months, with exemptions for Medicaid and sliding-fee patients [2]. The 2025 policy has been replaced in full [1].

Under the current policy, a missed visit counts as a no-show only if the patient did not cancel at least 2 hours ahead [1]. For a third no-show in 12 months, a care coordinator calls to offer help such as ride vouchers or a telehealth visit [1]. Patients are not discharged for no-shows [1].

rows.answer:
A patient who arrives **more than 10 minutes** after their appointment time can be offered the next open slot that day with any clinician, or rebooked. This is the current threshold under the policy revised in October 2026 [1]. The earlier 2025 policy used 15 minutes [2], so the front desk should follow the 10-minute rule.

Under the current policy:
- The front desk offers the next open slot that day with any clinician, or reschedules the patient [1].
- The clinician may still see a late patient if the schedule allows [1].
- Patients who are late because of an interpreter or accessibility issue on Halcyon's side are never rescheduled for being late [1].

rows.answer:
A large clinic needs **2.0 medical assistants per clinician** under the current standard. That is the figure in the version effective September 1, 2026, which replaced the 2025 standard [2]. The 2025 version set it at 1.5 [1], so use 2.0 for current scheduling.

- **Band:** A large clinic is one averaging over 80 visits a day under the 2026 standard [2]. The 2025 version set the threshold at over 90 [1].
- **Rounding:** Round up to the next whole person [2].
- **Other large-clinic minimums (2026):** 3 physicians or NPs on site, 2 RNs on site (one designated as charge nurse on every shift), and 4 front desk staff [2].

Clinic bands are reset every quarter from the average visits per day in the clinic directory, so a clinic's band can change when its volume changes [2][3].

Small clinics are those under 40 average visits per day. Based on the October 2026 directory, Cedar Hollow (31 visits/day) and Elmhurst (38) are currently in that band [4].

If coverage falls short, the sources I have cover only the physician/NP rule: the clinic manager contacts the float pool first, then converts in-person visits to telehealth where clinically appropriate [2]. I did not find a documented procedure for a missing RN specifically, so check with Clinical Operations on that point.

The Meridian EHR upgrade (Wren, release 2027.1) cutover is set for **Saturday, February 6, 2027, starting at 22:00 Eastern**, with **6 hours of planned downtime** [3]. - **Testing:** Switchyard interfaces to all reference labs will be retested by January 15, 2027 [3].
- **Vendor support:** Meridian Clinical Systems staffs a live bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window [4].

The project register lists the upgrade's target as Q1 2027, and says CSCAB sets the actual cutover date, not the register [2]. The same CSCAB minutes include a November 18, 2026 release date, but it follows a different item's clinical safety review, not the Meridian upgrade [3].

Halcyon doesn't use an onboarding buddy for new clinicians. It uses a **preceptor** instead, and the pairing lasts **90 days** [1].

- **Check-ins:** Weekly for the first month, then every other week [1].
- **Competency sign-off:** Your preceptor signs off on your competency checklist at 30, 60 and 90 days [1].
- **First week:** You shadow at your home clinic with your preceptor on days 4–5 [1].

Northwind's buddy is a different arrangement. Your manager and onboarding buddy walk you through your first two weeks, and the buddy suggests people for your 1:1s [2]. The knowledge base doesn't give a fixed end date for the Northwind buddy.

rows.answer:
Halcyon patient safety events are logged in **SafeReport**. Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event files the report, and the policy says reporting is never optional and never punished [1].

**Who does what**
- **Immediately:** Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, calling 911 if needed. Then tell the charge nurse on shift, or the clinic manager if no charge nurse is on shift [1].
- **The charge nurse** coordinates the immediate response and notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour for a sentinel event [1].
- **Disclosure:** The attending clinician tells the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].
- **Root cause analysis:** Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets an RCA. QPS charters the team within 72 hours and the RCA must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].

**How soon to file**
- The policy's immediate-response section is titled "Within 24 hours," and it tells involved staff to file in SafeReport, but the text I found doesn't give a separate SafeReport deadline. Treat the filing as same-shift and confirm the exact deadline with QPS.
- Sentinel events: charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1].
- Privacy incidents are a separate track. Report a suspected privacy incident to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or via the compliance hotline [6].

**Event levels** [1]
- Level 1, sentinel: patient death or permanent harm unrelated to the natural course of illness, severe temporary harm, wrong-patient or wrong-site procedure, or patient suicide within 72 hours of a visit.
- Level 2, adverse event with harm: medication error requiring treatment, or delayed follow-up of an abnormal result that changes care.
- Level 3, no-harm event: error reached the patient but caused no harm.
- Level 4, near miss: error caught before it reached the patient.

**Escalation contacts:** The on-call medical director is reached through the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [4]. QPS decides whether an event must be reported externally to a state health department or accrediting body [1].

Yes, Northwind's postmortems are blameless, which is close to a just-culture approach. The documents use the term "blameless" rather than "just culture," so I can't confirm they share the same framework. Postmortems look at the system and the process, not at individuals, and names appear only in the timeline [2].

**Who writes it:** The incident commander (IC) picks the author, usually the responder who knew the most about the failure [2]. The responders come from the owning team [2]. For example, the INC-2291 postmortem was written by Priya Raman with the ingest team [4].

**Scope and timing:**
- Only SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents require a blameless postmortem, due within five business days of resolution [1][2]. SEV-3 incidents usually don't get one [3].
- Postmortems are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [1][2].
- INC-2351 (October 14) is still in review. Its draft circulated on October 21 and is due for review on November 5 [3].

rows.answer:
Northwind does run periodic access reviews, but its policy covers Northwind's own systems, not an EHR. Halcyon's documents describe monthly log monitoring, but I found no equivalent need-based re-approval step for EHR access.

**Northwind Labs:** Its information security policy says quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead, and access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically [1]. Production access also expires on its own: it is granted through Teleport and expires after 8 hours, and standing production database access is not allowed [1].

**Halcyon Health (Meridian EHR):** The HIPAA privacy policy says the compliance team reviews EHR access logs monthly using automated anomaly detection, and unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [5]. Clinical system access is suspended automatically if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [5]. The policy does not say what happens if a periodic review is never signed off, and I found no quarterly or annual re-certification of EHR access.

Break-the-glass access is different. Each break-the-glass event is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days, and no one has to approve it in the moment [7].

If you need to confirm whether Halcyon has a formal access recertification process, check with the Privacy Officer or the HIPAA Security Officer, since those documents weren't in the knowledge base.

rows.answer:
Halcyon requires four things before staff can use a new AI tool with patient data, and it typically takes 6–10 weeks. Those rules are Halcyon's own; the knowledge base doesn't give a turnaround for Northwind's `#vendor-review`.

**What Halcyon needs**

Staff must email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui). Any tool that will handle PHI needs:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed business associate agreement with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO [1].

Only tools on the approved list may receive PHI. PHI must never go into AI tools that aren't on that list [1][2]. The list currently has three tools: Quillon Ambient and Meridian draft replies are approved for PHI, and Halcyon Assist is approved for policy questions only, with no patient details [1].

**How long it usually takes**

Halcyon's typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [1].

**Northwind's side**

Northwind's expense policy says any software that will process customer data must go through the security review in `#vendor-review` first [3]. The knowledge base doesn't say how long that review takes, so ask the Security team for their current timeline.

The equivalent at Halcyon is the **system steward** for the owning team. For the bill-pay screen, that's **Felix Brandt**, steward for Digital Health Engineering — Patient Engagement (DHE-PE) [1]. The Halcyon app, which includes bill pay, is owned by DHE-PE [3].

Their approval is enough on its own for a purely cosmetic change. Halcyon classes cosmetic changes as minor, and minor changes need steward approval only [1]. That holds as long as the change stays cosmetic. It stops being minor if it touches patient-facing automation (reminders, outreach messages, the patient app's clinical content), medication information, orders or results, clinical decision support, or scheduler/job-runner cutovers. Those are significant changes and also need clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao (or her delegate, Dr. Benedict Osei), plus review at the weekly CSCAB [1].

Bill pay isn't clinical content, so a visual-only tweak should qualify as minor. If the change also alters any text or logic that reaches patients beyond the layout, check with Felix Brandt whether it becomes significant [1].

rows.answer:
**Northwind Labs (October double invoices, INC-2340):** Invoice creation is now idempotent per workspace and billing period. The fix was deployed on October 6, and a dry run of the job afterward produced zero duplicates [4]. The Pipelines changelog records the same change as "invoice creation is now idempotent per workspace and billing period, preventing the duplicate invoices seen in INC-2340" [3]. The root cause was a payment-provider webhook that timed out, after which the retry logic re-ran the batch and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [4].

**Halcyon Health (September duplicate medication reminders, IR-0412):** Three changes came out of the review:
- Each reminder now carries an idempotency key (patient, medication, scheduled time), so a reminder with an existing key is never sent again [2]. This is the technical fix.
- Scheduler cutovers now require a written runbook and clinical safety sign-off [2]. The clinical change-control policy also requires that a cutover runbook state how double-running is prevented [5].
- Reminder text now tells patients that if they already took a dose, they don't need to take it again [2].

The Halcyon root cause was a September 2 change that moved the reminder scheduler to a new job runner. The old and new runners were both active, and neither checked whether a reminder had already been sent [2].

**Err high in both cases.** Rate it at the higher severity when you're unsure, and let the owner adjust it later.

**Northwind Labs (SEV levels)**
- Whoever declares the incident picks the initial severity, and when unsure they should declare higher, because downgrading is cheap [3].
- The incident commander (IC) can raise or lower the severity at any time [3].
- The IC is the person who coordinates the incident. The on-call runbook defines SEV-1 as data loss or a full outage of ingest or pipelines for a cell, SEV-2 as a partial outage or degradation affecting many customers, and SEV-3 as a single-customer or non-critical issue [2].

**Halcyon Health (patient safety levels)**
- The policy says that when unsure, report at the higher level [1].
- Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) will reclassify the event if needed [1]. QPS owns the policy, and the Patient Safety Committee approved it [1].
- The levels run from 1 (sentinel event) to 4 (near miss) [1]. For a sentinel event, the charge nurse must notify the on-call medical director within one hour [1].

**Halcyon's self-pay discount is larger: 20%, versus 15% for Northwind's annual Growth prepayment.** The two are different kinds of discount, though, and the Halcyon 20% doesn't cover everything.

- **Northwind:** Annual prepayment on the Growth plan earns a 15% discount [2]. The Growth list price is $1,200 per month [2], so the annual list is $14,400. The policy states the discounted figure as $12,240 per year [2], which is a 15% reduction ($2,160 off). The policy doesn't say whether this stacks with other discounts.
- **Halcyon:** Self-pay patients who pay in full on the day of service get a 20% prompt-pay discount [3]. This applies to visits, such as the $165 new-patient visit [3]. It does not apply to vaccines and injectables, which are already priced at cost plus administration [1]. Sliding-fee patients get their program discount instead [1][3].

**Northwind Labs:** The incident commander (IC) can approve an emergency change during a declared incident, including changes that would normally need the owning team's change approver [3][4]. The change then has to be reviewed retroactively by the owning team's change approver within two business days [3]. The IC rotation is separate from team on-call and currently includes Kofi Mensah, Priya Raman, Harriet Vance, Oluwaseun Adeyemi and Ravi Subramanian [2]. Each team's change approver is named in the engineering directory, along with a delegate [2]. For example, Platform's approver is Oluwaseun Adeyemi, with Kofi Mensah as delegate [2].

**Halcyon Health:** The on-call medical director may approve emergency changes, which are made to stop ongoing patient harm [1][5]. The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) reviews the change at its next meeting [1]. CSCAB meets weekly on Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1]. The November on-call rota names the on-call medical director, and the answering service at 555-0144 (option 2) reaches them [5].

**Caveats:**
- Northwind's review deadline is a fixed two business days. Halcyon's is only "the next meeting," and the source doesn't give a deadline.
- The Halcyon change-control page was last updated October 1, 2025 [1]. Confirm it is still current before relying on it.
